speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Etobicoke North.

As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the question of financial institutions raises basically the problems of solvency, the concerns about probity, the question of competition and, finally, the need for national control and ownership.
The way that Canada orders its financial institutions and markets to a surprisingly large extent influences the way that we order our national objectives. "By following the money flows in the market economy", one observer has noted, "and dissecting the institutions that structure
that flow, we can learn a great deal about the uses to which the society's resources are put, by whom, and how control is obtained and exerted." That is, in a sense, what we are doing today. We are discussing a fundamental question concerning the future of our country. It is that question that I wish to address today.
Allow me to begin with a question. How can our financial institutions best respond to the growing internationalization of markets and, more specifically, to the likely takeovers that will threaten Canadian control of its technology as well as its commercial and financial resources?
Over the years we have seen a variety of pressures for change arise in the Canadian economy that have led to the development of the legislation that is before us today. One of the principal forces that has made for change in financial institutions is inflation. The volatility of interest rates has led to shortening of the terms of both assets and liabilities in Canada, so as to reduce thereby the risks of borrowing at short term and lending at long term.
Over a period of time, with the shortening of terms of lending in Canada, institutions formerly active in longterm instruments have sought out increasingly shortterm funds. They have sought a better matching of their obligations and of their assets. That has led to a crowding in the short-term intermediation of financial dealings. It has contributed directly to the blurring of the four institutions that we have traditionally recognized in Canada; the brokerage houses, the banks, the insurance companies and the trust companies. That blurring of institutions has in turn led to increasing problems of regulation. Obviously, if institutions become blurred, more indistinct than they traditionally have been, problems of regulation arise.
Equally, when we recognized in Canada some years ago the necessity of increasing deposit insurance, one result was that trust companies had their way opened to participate yet more actively in the total area of financial intermediation. The Bank Act revisions of 1954 and 1967 only increased the blurring of distinctions among the so-called four pillars of the financial world by allowing the banks first into consumer loans and subsequently into mortgages.
November 6, 1990

The result of this has been that the banks have become increasingly active in areas that had hitherto been the preserve of trust companies. Equally, as I mentioned, as a result of increased deposit insurance, the trust companies have become more and more active in deposit taking, an area that had traditionally been the preserve of our chartered banks.
Yet more recently, we have seen the entry of banks into the brokerage business. A few years ago the government, partly in response to an initiative taken by a chartered bank, enabled the banks not only to enter into the brokerage business, but to acquire the assets of brokerage companies. The consequence is that today there are, in effect, no major independent brokerage houses. That fourth pillar of our traditional financial community has now disappeared, in the sense of being an independent or stand alone entity.
Also, Mr. Speaker, over the years we have seen regulatory change leading to pressures for further regulatory change. You begin to change one regulation and you find soon that you must respond to other changes that are demanded as a result of the first change you made. So we have pressures from the mere fact that over a period of decades Canada changed its regulation of financial institutions, but that has led in turn to yet more demands for change.
The parallel to that has been that the provinces' increased activity in financial regulation. The provinces have been more active in their imaginative approaches to financial intermediation, both with regard to deposittaking institutions, that is trust companies, banks and co-operatives, and in the regulation of insurance and other financial activities which were traditionally the preserve of the federal government.
Another factor that has made for increased blurring of distinctions among financial institutions and, hence, increased the pressures for a re-examination of the regulation of financial institutions has been the globalization of financial companies.
We have seen the changes that have been introduced in other countries leading to pressures for change in Canada. I speak not merely of the United States, although the implications of the free trade agreement for financial institutions are many, but also of recent initiatives in Europe which have had the effect of
Government Orders
reducing the distinctions among financial institutions. This in turn has contributed to similar pressures in Canada so that Canadian financial institutions can compete internationally on what has been called a level playing field.
I spoke of solvency being one of the primary concerns. Today it remains a concern that all our financial institutions serving the public can guarantee their solvency through good business practices but this leads to the yet more basic question of whether banks should be regulated. The essence of that question is: Do you regulate institutions when institutions are becoming increasingly indistinct, or do you regulate the activity itself? The legislation we have before us today chooses to go mainly along that second route.
We have also seen the standards of competition and efficiency being applied to our financial institutions in terms of whether they are internationally competitive. We have seen questions arise of whether there are more possibilities of conflict of interest in the growing combination of financial institutions. We have seen concern expressed increasingly and, most recently, in the case of the entry of Amex into Canadian banking, about the role of foreign corporations in what hitherto has been largely a Canadian dominated industry.
There is yet a more fundamental question. The relative importance of direct financing through equity markets has declined over the years. There has been greater reliance on financial intermediation through credit from financial institutions such as banks and trust companies. That trend has been increasing. We also saw in Canada a rapid growth in demand in the 1980s for consumer and mortgage loans and a shift by non-financial corporations away from bond and equity financing to bank loans. As I have already noted, the increased level and volatility of inflation and interest rate uncertainty led both borrowers and lenders to turn to shorter term liabilities and assets, providing trust and loan companies with a new competitive niche in the total lending market.
Legislative changes have led to increased competition across traditional institutional lines. The lowering of reserve requirements on banks' term deposits and the removal of ceilings on bank loan rates improved their ability to compete for term deposits. The increased competition in deposit markets forced financial institutions to extend and diversify their range of services.

November 6, 1990
Government Orders
As I noted a moment ago, all these and other factors, have led to the situation today where Canadians must ask themselves-and the government has raised the question directly by tabling its legislation-which route, and they are not necessarily exclusive, Canada wants to follow with regard to our financial institutions. If the goal is indeed deregulation of financial institutions, we can move toward commercial links. That is to say, through legislation, the government can permit companies to hold upstream financial institutions. You can then have in Canada, as we have seen developing in the last years, a commercial company holding upstream the ownership of a financial institution. That is a relatively new feature of the Canadian financial scene and one which this legislation, to a degree, attempts to address.
The alternative, and again I say it is not necessarily mutually exclusive, is the financial link approach. That is to say, the government can permit downstream holdings of commercial entities by financial institutions, principally the banks. As a result, if the banks were permitted to engage in activities and hold equity in commercial corporations, as they so frequently do in Europe and Japan, then Canada would obviously emerge with institutions not unlike the so-called "universal banks" of Europe.
The merit of such an approach, in the eyes of some, is that it would help guarantee Canadian ownership, not only of our principal financial institutions but also of manufacturing or service industries generally. On the other hand, the price that concerns others is the lack of competition to which that could give rise. The result could be larger and larger Canadian conglomerates, bringing with them misgivings about the limited degree of competition within our economy.
The creation of financial links, that is Canadian banks or trust companies holding equity in commercial corporations, could be argued to be in Canada's basic national interest. The government would then presumably need to consider a type of financial regulation whereby widely held financial institutions, which are at present only the chartered banks, limited as they are to 10 per cent ownership by any one entity, could enter the commercial sector.
Financial links along such lines would undoubtedly ease the evolution toward a credit based rather than a market based financial system. That is to say, commercial entities within our country would seek their financing more from financial institutions than they would from the equity marketplace. Not only would such a trend be compatible with the general thrust of the evolution of money markets world-wide, but it could also give Canada a more long-range and stable element in industrial planning.
Most important, by permitting financial links the government could be instituting one means of keeping Canadian assets in Canadian hands. If the concern among Canadians is that many Canadian assets have for past decades been moving gradually out of Canadian control, then banks, which are by definition widely held, could be a vehicle whereby Canadians could retain a controlling interest in a Canadian commercial institution, rendering it virtually takeover-proof by foreign interests.
Against that speculative background, I want to speak for a moment more about the legislation before us today, recognizing that its emphasis is to take Canada's financial institutions in a direction rather different from that which I have just touched upon. The bill empowers trust companies to a point where in many respects they will be able to compete yet more effectively and pervasively with banks. Well capitalized trust companies will have full consumer and commercial lending powers for the first time, putting them on virtually the same level as our banks.
I believe that it is clause 400 in the legislation that removes the present quality tests and substitutes instead a requirement that a company's investment adhere to a prudent portfolio standard. There is, however, no limit on consumer loans under $250,000 made to individuals. Similarly, subject to the approval of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, companies with more than $25 million in capital will be free of any restrictions on commercial lending.
The bill permits trust and loan companies to engage in a limited range of non-financial services for the first time or extends their ability to engage in such services: real property management, promotion of goods and services to credit card holders, selling lottery and even urban transit tickets. The principal extension in this bill is opening the way for deposit taking institutions to enter the life insurance business. Here of course is a major
November 6, 1990

change, a major erosion of the four pillars that we have traditionally known in Canadian financial institutions. For the first time, the possibility is that Canadian deposit taking institutions will be able to participate directly in the insurance business.
The question that I would raise here is: What studies has the government prepared? What has it done in the way of examining the results of insurance companies being in the hands of the deposit taking institutions?
I hope the government would table whatever work it has done in this area, because I have an uneasy feeling that it is not very much. All Canadians would benefit if we could see more information about what work the government has done to determine the public interest in insurance companies being opened to ownership by financial institutions.
I realize that my time is running out. I only want to say in conclusion that the trust companies bill which we have before us also raises the question of limitations of ownership. The banks are subjected to a 10 per cent ownership limit. This bill, however, confirms that commercial entities can own trust companies up to a level of 65 per cent; 35 per cent must be held more widely.
Whether in the view of the Canadian public this is an adequate guarantee of their interests in ensuring probity and good business practices in financial institutions remains a question for further debate in committee. It is a question which will arise again when the next Bank Act revision comes before the House, and indeed when the revisions to the Life Insurance Act come before this House, two further occasions that will give rise to the sort of discussions we are having today. Indeed, until then the present legislation, even if adopted at an early date, will not become effective. I look forward to further discussions on those occasions.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the member would comment on this particular question. In this bill we have a situation where, as a result of the free trade agreement, Schedule II banks from the United States can come into Canada and do all the things that Schedule A banks can do, that our banks can do. Yet they are not bound by the 10 per cent ownership rule.
Government Orders
Does the member feel that this is an acceptable treatment of a foreigner, treating them one way, which is different from the way the Canadian would be treated?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member does indeed put his finger on a major policy flaw in the government's approach to financial institutions. The tip of the iceberg was the approval of the Amex Bank entry into Canada. Here we have a foreign institution, which is not primarily a bank in its domestic jurisdiction, being permitted to act as a bank in Canada when Canadians are denied a similar opportunity.
Whether you think that the commercial entities in Canada should be permitted to own banks is another question, but it remains a remarkable anomaly, not to say a bizarre anomaly, that you permit a foreign non-bank to be a bank in Canada.
I agree with the hon. member that the free trade agreement provisions, whereby Canada has opened the way for American financial activity in Canada to a degree which Canadians do not have in the United States, is patently unfair.
What the government did in the free trade agreement was to offer American financial institutions so-called national treatment in return for the United States offering Canadian financial institutions national treatment in the United States. However, the difference is that in the United States the banks are state regulated, whereas in Canada banks are federally regulated. The result is that American financial institutions are able to participate on a national level in Canada, whereas a Canadian financial institution is restricted, with some qualification, to one state.
I would have thought-and I am sure that the hon. member would agree-that the government, in the free trade agreement, should not have sought national treatment but rather sought greater reciprocity so that Canadian financial institutions operating in the United States could have comparable opportunities to those that American financial institutions do in Canada.
I think the point is quite well taken, but it should be directed to the government.

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, because the hon. member is so knowledgeable in this field, I thought I should follow up with a supplementary question.
Since I know he has read this bill and is familiar with it, is it not possible under this bill-here is where the thing gets even more ludicrous-that a Canadian with lots of bucks can actually go into the United States, buy a bank and then bring that bank into Canada as a Schedule II bank and do all the things that our banks do here, and yet avoid the ownership rule? Is it not possible?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether there are any regulations that would prevent a Canadian citizen from doing that. It is one more anomaly that we have gotten ourselves into not only through our own legislation but also through the free trade agreement with the United States.
The opportunity for the hon. member, myself or for anyone interested in this question-all Canadians should be-to raise it again will occur when the decennial Bank Act is brought before this House.
Recently the government acted to extend for one year the Bank Act beyond its normal decennial period. Whether we shall have that opportunity for further debate before the government changes, I do not know. It is yet another example of the inconsistency of our approach to foreign ownership of Canadian financial institutions.
The hon. member is probably quite right. I suppose on the face of it, there is no reason why, if a well-financed Canadian could buy a U.S. bank, he or she could not come back into Canada as a foreign bank operating in Canada, and do things that he or she, as a Canadian, could not do.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville-Visible Minorities; the hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau-Unemployment Insurance; and finally the hon. member for Saint-Leonard-The Economy.

Mr. Speaker, we have the first piece of legislation in front of us with Bill C-83 which makes up the government's package of financial deregulation measures.
This is a package which will include action not just with respect to trust and loan institutions, but also with respect to banks, insurance companies, extension of the Bank Act and a number of other financial institutions which have been of concern to business people. It is not just the business people but communities across this country that have been looking for this package of reforms to our financial institutions for some time.
My own suspicion is that this first piece of legislation is, in fact, put before us in a form which will not in the final analysis represent what the government wishes to have considered for reform in terms of trust and loan companies.
I suspect myself that this has been brought forward in a sense as a promise to financial circles within the country that the government is acting in this area where it has not seemed to be taking action very quickly. We will, in fact, see a package which will include a similar approach to the different financial institutions which will probably include a revised piece of legislation with respect to trust and loan companies.
However, I think that the broad direction which the government is taking with respect to financial institutional reform is fairly clear to see. It is a direction which was set out by the junior finance minister in his comments when this bill was introduced. It is an approach which we have discussed in the finance committee of the House in somewhat more detail in the context of briefings which have been given to us by representatives from the Department of Finance.
The key thrusts of the government's new approach, as the minister laid them out and as they seem to be reflected in the briefings that we have received are, first, that we shall see some quite different ownership rules for financial institutions. There will be a good deal of loosening up of the constraints which have existed in the past, as far as ownership constraints are concerned. We will see, for instance, a loosening up with respect to the involvement of foreigners within our country. We will see, as a consequence of the free trade deal which my colleague mentioned earlier, that United States financial
November 6, 1990

institutions are treated virtually as if they were Canadian financial institutions. That is going to be one set of new directions.
The second set of new directions is to reduce the barriers which have existed in the past among the various financial institutions in this country. It has not been possible, for instance, for insurance companies to have investments in banks in the past. It has not been possible for banks to have investments in insurance companies. Similarly, trust and loan companies have been given certain specific tasks which they could undertake and they have been told that they could not extend their ownership to other forms of financial institutions, such as securities houses, such as insurance companies and banks. So that is going to change.
Third, there is going to be a set of what the government calls improved prudential rules. What, in fact, are improved prudential rules? They are, essentially, an approach which, as I read it, puts much more self-policing power in the hands of financial institutions themselves. Financial institutions are given the authority and the responsibility to make certain that there is no internal self-dealing. They are given the responsibility to see to it that, for instance, if there is cross-ownership, that that cross-ownership of other financial institutions does not lead to special, competitive advantages as a consequence. I have to say that this self-policing approach is something which we look at with considerable scepticism. Frankly, we are not prepared to condemn it outright at this point, but we will ask some very tough questions as this reform of financial institutions goes forward, because we think it represents an area of serious risk for this country and for the people who put their investments in the various financial institutions.
Finally, the government says that this is an attempt to modernize the company rules which exist for the various financial institutions. By and large, that is not something that provides special difficulties for us. This particular legislation has not been changed since the beginning of the First World War. There are all sorts of potential areas for modernization of company legislation which should be applied to this financial area of jurisdiction within our economy.
Government Orders
That is the government's approach. What about the Liberal Party's approach? You might have thought from listening to the last speaker, who is the trade critic for the Liberal Party that, in fact, the Liberal Party had considerable doubts and was raising considerable questions about this piece of legislation. In fact, the critic responsible for financial institutions for the Liberal Party made it very clear in her comments, when she started debate on behalf of the Liberals, that the Liberal Party favours this piece of legislation.
It is especially interesting to see why this deregulation was favoured by the Liberal Party.
Tell us about your program of nationalizing banks.

We are coming to my program. Do not worry about that. Do not be sensitive. You should be proud of the position which your critic took. The Liberal Party's critic said they favour this bill because globalization is taking place, that world globalization was a new reality, and because of globalization, it is necessary to help Canadian financial institutions to meet tougher competition. That is precisely the sort of message which the government itself sent. So in the crucial area of economic management, as in so many important areas, one finds that the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party stand for essentially the same thing. They both support the deregulation of financial institutions. They both support it for essentially the same reason; because there is globalization taking place and our financial institutions have to become tougher and stronger and have to be better able to fight the rest of the world.
Let me make some points about this approach from both the Conservatives and the Liberals. We should not be prepared to permit the two business-oriented parties in the House of Commons simply to rewrite legislation without a quarrel, without being challenged when that legislation is, in fact, going to be so detrimental, in our view, to many consumers across this country.
Let me suggest, that it is important, for instance, to look very carefully at the fact that since 1980, in less than 10 years, 23 trust and loan companies in the country have been federally chartered. In addition, since 1980, a great number of trust companies have collapsed.

November 6, 1990
Government Orders
I could go through the list of some of the larger ones just to demonstrate it. The Crown Trust Company collapsed with an estimated loss of $930 million; Fidelity Trust, $791 million; Greymac Trust Company, $240 million; Seaway Trust, $300 million; Pioneer Trust, $201 million; the Columbia Trust, $99 million; the Northwest Trust Company, which collapsed just in 1987, $275 million; and finally, perhaps the most scandalous case of all, the Principal Savings and Trust Company, which collapsed in 1987 with losses of $116 million.
With these kinds of disasters which our trust and loan companies have suffered in recent years, it is not good enough to stand up and say: "We support this legislation", as the Liberals have done. It is not good enough, as the Conservatives have done, to bring forth legislation which leaves it to self-policing to see to it that things will work out well in the future for those who invest in our trust companies.
We also see within this bill absolutely nothing with respect to disclosure of the various service charges of trust and loan companies. In the case of banks, the government says it is going to enforce such disclosure of service payments. But in the case of trust and loan companies, despite quite ambiguous legal advice, the government is not prepared to take the chance, despite the fact that trust and loan companies compete directly against chartered banks in the country. Again, it is not good enough on the part of the Liberals and the Conservatives to say this is an answer, when there is nothing in here about disclosure of service charges.
It seems to us quite clear that this legislation is set up in such a way as to assist financial institutions to take each other over, but to prevent those financial institutions from all-out competition with each other. In other words, this is a bill designed to see to it that the financial institutions involved in this bill have their cake and get to eat it too.
In short, this legislation is going to establish, without question, greater financial monopoly throughout the country. It will not be with this piece of legislation alone, but it will be with the whole package of financial deregulation which the Conservatives are putting into effect and which, so far, the Liberals are supporting. We are going to see greater monopoly control.
We are also going to see a situation established in which all-out competition is not possible. It will not be possible in this approach by the Conservatives and Liberals for financial institutions to compete with each other. In their support for this legislation, we are getting from the Liberals and Conservatives the worst of all possible worlds. Therefore, we intend to oppose this piece of legislation. We intend to raise very tough questions in committee and we intend to see to it that this legislation is given the kind of scrutiny which eventually gives Canadian consumers across the country a sense of real competition amongst their financial institutions.
We also intend to see to it that there is real security given to those people who invest in our banks and our trust and loan companies so that we do not have, as we have had since 1980, a total of almost $5 billion in losses on the part of our banks and our trust and loan companies. Consumers deserve competition to give them protection and investors deserve serious regulation to give them protection as well.

Mr. Speaker, I was quite impressed by the ability of our debator to wait until the last 30 seconds to give us an opportunity to understand the issues that he wanted to address in the debate. I am impressed that he was able to repeat what members from my caucus, over the course of the debate on Bill C-83, have indicated are very essential elements of rectifying the legislation before us. That is, ensuring that there is security of deposits for depositors, that there is better service available to those who are going to be dependent on the financial service sector, and that there will be an opportunity to enhance the ability of all those pillars to compete on the domestic front and on the international front.
One of the questions I would ask the hon. member for Essex-Windsor this. Does he not think that it diminishes the import of those very basic and solid principles by distracting not only the House, but all those who would want to understand better the flow of debate on this very important legislation? He has trivialized the discussion and made references to incomplete statements that he picks and chooses from debate of members on both sides of the House.
His major concern with respect to this legislation is not that we can bring it forward to committee, analyse it, dissect it, critique it, and bring forward the appropriate amendments to make it something that Canadians can feel comfortable with. In fact, his big concern is that the

Liberal Party has made the kind of recommendations that cause him some consternation and, in fact, that the Liberal Party might be in a position to present the kinds of amendments that he would so dearly love to support.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals get themselves into this problem so often. Their official position before they start debate is that they support the bill. They think it is a good thing, and it is because of international competition. Their critic gets up and says so. We get up and make our criticisms and comments, as my colleague who is responsible for financial institutions made in his original speech. Then the Liberals start to back-track and say: "Gee, we forgot about some key elements here. We had better flip through this bill really carefully and see if Rodriguez was right." In fact of course, as usual, my colleague from Nickel Belt was right, because he and I have been at the finance committee. We have been working quite hard trying, right from the ground up, to improve the approach that the government has taken.
I certainly hope very much that the Liberals will come forward and make some amendments. Frankly, they have put themselves in a difficult position through the fact that their critic got up and said that they favoured this bill. In favouring this bill, they make it quite clear that, as I suggested in my comments, the parties that are oriented to big business in the country both feel supportive of this legislation.
Well, we make no apologies for not being supportive of this bill. Our critic said that when he got up to speak and it has been the position of our caucus right from our analysis of the bill itself.
If it is possible to improve the bill in committee, of course that is useful. As I suggested and as the trade critic of the Liberal Party agreed, this piece of legislation before us is in all probability just a stalking horse. It is just a preliminary piece of legislation to tell the financial community: "Don't worry, guys. There is something coming that will cover the whole range of institutions."
Let us talk about the whole range of institutions. Let us see to it that we get it right. Let us not accept a faulty
Government Orders
approach which is going to leave consumers unprotected and those who invest in these institutions without the security which good solid regulation would give them. That is why we are against this bill and we will fight it at this stage of second reading.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to my colleague present such an excellent expose of the bill and, of course, clearly repeating the line that the New Democratic Party has taken about its concerns on Bill C-83, I want to ask him this particular question.
In this bill the government is finally going to put into effect regulations, rules, a law concerning bank service charges. Lo and behold, trust and loan companies are going to be allowed to act and perform like banks. Yet, Bill C-83 is unable to impose on trust and loan companies such a pussy-cat proposal as envisaged in Bill C-9 on the trust and loan companies. The government is using weasel words like: "Well, we can't impose these bank service charge rules on trust and loan companies because they are in another jurisdiction."
What confidence does that inspire in consumers? In fact, trust companies and loan companies can draw on the CDIC, which is the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. Most of those who have drawn from that have been trust companies because those are the ones that have gone belly up. Yet, we cannot say to trust companies: "You jolly well will be subject to the bank service charges legislation if you want to continue to participate in the CDIC." Where is the logic?
There is none.

Mr. Speaker, I think that my colleague has picked up an important point which both he and I made earlier in our speeches.
That is both the Conservatives and the Liberals are supporting legislation which does not follow any logic. There is a complete lack of logic to say that banks and trust and loan companies on the one hand should be able to compete better against each other and they should be able to buy each other out to a certain degree.

Government Orders
Yet, on the other hand, to say we will have disclosure rules with respect to service charges or banks, but we will not have disclosure rules with respect to trust and loan companies, is illogical.
It is even more illogical than that because the government has seen fit to say that it will enforce disclosure rules with respect to interest rates on the trust and loan companies. It will not enforce those disclosure rules on what are often substitutes for interest levies, that is the service charges which trust and loan companies levy just as banks levy.
There has to be a logic to this legislation if it is to be accepted by this House and by this country. Otherwise, we will see more and more bank, loan and trust company collapses of the kind that this government across the aisle has seen take place under its jurisdiction and which the Liberals saw take place under their jurisdiction prior to 1984.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. members across the way for this tremendous vote of confidence which they just gave me, all two of them.
It is interesting that we should be talking partly about bank service charges because I just said to the hon. member for Nickel Belt that the way the banks are going, you can hardly walk by the outside of a bank these days without having a service charge debited to your account.
I grew up at a time when we still believed, at least the popular mythology was, that the banks were there to serve the public. There were these respectable dour institutions that Stephen Leacock made famous and which was later turned into an animated film of people going into the bank and being very respectful.
Now, of course, those of us who still go in and tiy to have some genuine human relationship instead of going to a machine are forced to pay for every time that we do this. Of course, they will set up a chequing account and then you are not charged for writing cheques, but you are charged for the cheques.
In the end, what it amounts to is that somehow they get you. Somehow you are paying for everything that allegedly the bank is doing for you. You are in fact paying for it.
In my riding, there was a branch of the Toronto-Domi-nion Bank at the Kern Park Shopping Centre which served the entire east end of Transcona. It was there for years, since the houses started to go up in that end of town. It not only shut that down, but the main branch in the town of Transcona lost the commercial banking which was shoved miles down the highway around to Kildonan Place shopping centre.
Now all the merchants in that place, used to dealing with that bank for years and years, are being forced to travel a great distance in order to serve the convenience of the bank. I am told it is not working out that well, which is good, and it may be that they might move back. Hopefully they will reopen the branch at Kern Park but they have not done that so far. All they have set up is some kind of remote teller, I am told, which is really handy for senior citizens to have to stand at some remote teller out in 40 below temperatures in the winter trying to figure out which buttons to push.
This is the kind of service we have been getting from the banks lately. It does not surprise me, therefore, that Canadians are not as disturbed as they should be when they hear that perhaps the government will be allowing others to enter more and more into the kind of services that banks provide.
There is a concern there, as members from Nickel Belt and Essex-Windsor have pointed out. If you are going to have institutions like trust and loan companies behaving like banks, they ought to be regulated like banks, which is a point that the banks make as well and something that certainly has a certain amount of internal coherence to it as an argument.
I think one of the things that we should be concerned about here as we enter into this first in a series, as I understand it, of bills having to do with the deregulation of the financial institutional sector is that this government has learned absolutely nothing about the effects of deregulation. It is embarrassing as a Canadian to have this sort of mimicking of what goes on in the United States happening all the time in Canada. You know, whatever was the fad 10 years ago in the United States, give it enough time and it becomes the fad here.
That would be bad enough, except that generally just as the fad is catching on here, the Americans are catching on that what we are about to imitate is not working. This is true of airline deregulation, and it is also
November 6, 1990

Government Orders
true of financial deregulation, not to mention a few other sectors that have been deregulated. I will resist the temptation to go on about rail deregulation.
The fact of the matter is that in the United States where this kind of deregulation has already taken place, we have seen the result. The savings and loans scandal has robbed hundreds of thousands of ordinary American citizens of their savings, of their life's work so to speak, as a result of the government eliminating by legislation their responsibility to ensure that companies into which ordinary Americans, in our case Canadians, entrust their savings, that the companies act in a way that does not put at risk those savings. Yet that is just the kind of thing through deregulation that the government is now contemplating in its own way.
The same thing has happened with airline deregulation. Airline deregulation has not been what it was touted to be. It has resulted in less public safety. It has resulted in worse service for a great many cities and regions of the United States. Yet we are imitating that in Canada. Soon we are going to find that airline deregulation did not result in increased competition and all of the things that have been said for it. We are going to end up with one airline with a monopoly over everything. They have learned nothing.
They have learned nothing from airline deregulation, they have learned nothing about the extent to which deregulation is not the panacea that so many people make it out to be, that it does not lead to this sort of orgy of competition that benefits the consumers. What it does lead to is an orgy of shenanigans between one institution and another, between various kinds of corporate monkeys who find various ways to screw the public and line their own pockets. That is what deregulation amounts to. It is an abdication of the government's responsibility to ensure that if we are going to have a marketplace society, that market operates in certain ways and operates in ways which protect Canadians who would trust their savings to those particular institutions. We do not want to be right about this, just as we did not want to be right about airlines deregulation and about rail deregulation, that it would mean a decrease rather than an increase in rail traffic. But it has meant a decrease in rail traffic because deregulation has lead to the increased use of trucks and this has environmental and public safety consequences.
Right now, near my riding, at Symington yard, you could fire a cannon through those marshalling yards and not be worried about hitting a boxcar because of the continuous erosion, policy-driven by this government, of the use of rail to move products in this country.
We see this result; it was predictable. We are predicting here today that deregulation of financial institutions will lead to some comparable disaster down the road for the public. It is not predictable in its detail but predictable in its certainty that someday we will rue the fact that the government has embarked on this abdication of responsibility. It is not complete abdication; there are rules and regulations and there are new rules and regulations but it is part of a process, part of an over-all philosophy on the part of this government, which says: "We trust the private sector. Those nice fellows out there would never put at risk the savings of senior citizens. They would never put at risk the financial well-being of ordinary Canadian families. They are a good bunch of guys; we do not have to watch them; they will police themselves".
This kind of naivety, and one is never sure whether it is naivety or deliberate, contrived stupidity, is the kind of thing that gets a lot of Canadians into trouble because they still trust that the government feels some residual responsibility for their financial well-being and that it would not allow banks, trust companies, and loan companies to really rip them off or to really put at risk their savings.
That trust is misplaced. It was trust that was misplaced to the extent that there were Canadians who trusted this government not to cut a bad deal with the United States over the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Trust was misplaced in a variety of other ways where Canadians could not really bring themselves to believe that any, duly elected, Canadian government would actually sell them down the river. And yet, that is exactly what happened with the Canada-U.S. Free Tirade Agreement. That is what has happened with airline deregulation and, in particular, in smaller towns and cities which now have less service and inferior service to what they had before. And it is certainly true with respect to transportation deregulation as a whole and the way in which our highways are now being clogged by more and more trucks. Just the other day, Mr. Speaker, I was on my way

to the airport and a truck went by which was almost as long as a train. It had two units.

new car lots of the country, but they also came a-knock-ing when it looked like the banks were going to be able to lease cars directly, which this bill does not permit. But it does permit a certain kind of leasing.
In both cases the foot is in the door. In both cases the banks have received what they wanted and are well on their way to the one-stop shopping for various financial services that they wanted to get. I think that is regrettable because, if we are going to have a competitive financial sector, we should not have departed from the traditional four pillars of the financial sector in this country and allowed them all to collapse into each other, and particularly allowed them to collapse into each other in a way that will permit more foreign ownership.
I was interested in the question that the hon. member for Nickel Belt posed to the Liberal member of Parliament who was speaking.
Liberal banker.
The Liberal banker who was speaking, that great Liberal who is actually-
A Tory.

A Tory who is more at home in terms of financial policy with the government. This is not a secret. This is well known to all, except perhaps the hon. member who continues to be a Liberal in spite of himself. That is not unusual, is it, for Liberals? They are able to swallow not just any sort of twist or manipulation.
Themselves.

They are also able to swallow themselves entirely on occasion, as the leader of the Liberal Party recently did on the GST.
The question, though, that was asked was: Could Canadians, who would not be permitted to do something as Canadians, do something if they were able to disguise themselves as Americans? By buying an American financial institution they would be able to do things in Canada, because it was American, that they would not be allowed to do if that same kind of institution was Canadian owned. What was the answer? Yes.
This is a very strange form of national treatment. National treatment generally means that you will treat someone from another country the same way that you would treat your own nations. What we find in this anomaly is not national treatment, but discrimination in favour of non-nationals so that people can do things in

Canada, if somehow they cannot be Canadian, which they could not do if they were Canadian.
This takes the special relationship that the Prime Minister promised that he would establish with the United States of America when he was elected in 1984 to new heights or depths, depending on your interpretation. What is not possible for Canadians will be possible for Canadians if somehow they have enough money to buy an American company to do in Canada what they would not be able to do if they had a Canadian company which was the very same.
Obviously there are a lot of problems with this deregulation initiative at the philosophical level. The fact is that the government seems to have learned nothing from the empty promises of deregulation which we have seen unfulfilled in other areas. I am sure some very real problems of detail, policy and regulations will be uncovered and, I hope, addressed adequately in committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to support the motion by the hon. member for Hillsborough, as amended to emphasize that Charlottetown should be recognized as the birthplace of Confederation and not of Canada.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this initiative is intended to mark the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of the 1864 Charlottetown Conference.
I have no quarrel with providing an official designation to mark the events that took place in this city in September 1864. The importance of the decisions that were made and their impact on our common destiny should be recognized by all Canadians.
However, we must not forget that Upper and Lower Canada were founded in 1791, nearly a century before the Charlottetown Conference. In fact, well before that date, the word "Canada" had been used by Jacques Cartier when on August 13, 1535, two young Indians in his company told him how to get to "Canada"; they were referring to the village of Stadacona, on the present site of Quebec City.
In fact, if we read official correspondence at the time, we find that the name Canada was synonymous with New France. However, in 1763, Great Britain dropped the name New France, using the designation Province of Quebec instead. The fact remains, however, that Canada designated, first of all, a geographic area washed by the waters of the St. Lawrence.
Canada was designated as such by the Constitutional Act, 1791. A considerably larger Quebec was divided into the provinces of Lower Canada and Upper Canada. In 1841, the two provinces were united as the Province of Canada. You will agree this was well before 1864.
Mr. Speaker, I add these few details because I want to give Quebec the place it deserves-its true status as the birthplace of Canada.
The Charlottetown Conference was indeed a crucial moment in our history. It acted as a catalyst, uniting strong forces that until then had been active, but in isolation, in the colonies of British North America.
It was a first step toward building a modem nation and ultimately, led to its gradual expansion from coast to coast.
When on September 1,1864, Charlottetown welcomed representatives of the United Province to the conference, it opened the way to union with the other colonies of British North America. A month later, this new spirit of co-operation was further expressed at the Quebec Conference, where those who would henceforth be called the Fathers of Confederation continued the work begun in Charlottetown.
They agreed on 72 resolutions, the so-called Quebec resolutions, which would form the basis for a union that would be officially recognized on July 1, 1867, by the British North America Act.
However, Mr. Speaker, without those initial steps in Charlottetown, subsequent developments would never have been possible. I am therefore pleased to support a proposal to designate Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation. Thanks to the federative pact that came out of this conference, Canada, after having been first a French and then a British colony, was able to become the vast country that has aroused the admiration of so many people throughout the world.
Perhaps I may quote a comment by U.S. historian S.E. Morrison, who said that never since the Roman Empire had local designations expanded so far beyond their original territory as did Canada and the St. Lawrence.
In 1989, we celebrated the anniversary of the conference where the foundation of Confederation was laid. Charlottetown has every reason to be proud of giving birth to a political and administrative superstructure, to which each member freely agreed to belong.
As the birthplace of Confederation, Charlottetown will remind us of the seeds of unity it sowed in our common history.
Although the capital of Prince Edward Island belongs above all to its inhabitants, in a broader sense it also belongs to all Canadians. That is why, Mr. Speaker, we want to stress its historical value, and I also think it would be a good opportunity to recall the principles that formed and continue to form the basis of our evolution as a nation.
November 6, 1990

Briefly, they can be identified as follows: liberty, diversity and solidarity.
Liberty first of all, because, as I said earlier, today's Canada was bom of a union that was entered into by free agents. In 1864 as in 1867, every member of that union believed, and history has borne this out, that they were right to do what they did and that united they would be strong.
Diversity-and I think it is appropriate to remember this, Mr. Speaker-because the British North America Act recognized the distinct identity of Quebec society by creating its own territory and recognizing its Civil Code, its language and its religion.
Finally, solidarity, because it and it alone has ensured that liberty and diversity have become a fact of life in Canada. Without the spirit of solidarity that inspired our ancestors, Canada would not have been able to deal as effectively with the problems it faced at the time. Although today's challenges may be different, I am sure that a belief in the principles established by the Fathers of Confederation will help us meet these challenges as well.
We Canadians, as human beings and with our legacy of diversity, have forged common traits and common values that today form the very essence of our national identity. Liberty, diversity and solidarity-sharing good times and bad, glory and despair, joy and sorrow.
I think this permanent commemoration of the 125th anniversary of the Charlottetown Conference of the Fathers of Confederation would be a good way to remember its guiding principles. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to reiterate my support for this proposal to designate Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation, because this city has played an important role, both tangible and symbolic, in this great adventure we call Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take very great pleasure in the opportunity to speak on this private members' motion of the hon. member from Prince Edward Island. Coming from New Brunswick, a sister province of Prince Edward Island and one of those provinces which joined with Prince Edward Island and the rest of Canada in 1864 to talk about the
Private Members' Business
idea of Confederation, I am particularly honoured tonight to participate in the debate on this resolution to pay tribute to Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation. It is with great pride that I stand before my colleagues to say a few words about the events that led to the birth of our nation.
Coincidentally, I am told that it was on this date, November 6, 1867, that Canada's Parliament was convened in session for the very first time. It is a particularly significant afternoon.
To remember our past is no mere exercise in nostalgia. It is a way of understanding who we are as a people and where we are going. I am reminded of the words of Canon Lionel Groulx, the prominent historian from Montreal, who wrote: "A nation cannot separate itself from its past any more than a river can separate itself from its source. No generation is self-sufficient."
It is good and it is important to take a long-range view of Canada. We should realize that the constitutional discussions of 1990 arise from the vibrant passages from our history books. Their origins lie in those very first exercises in consensus building conducted by the Fathers of Confederation almost 125 years ago.
What happened in those early days of Confederation and what is happening now are part of a continuum in all parts of an ongoing effort to work through our differences and to find mutually acceptable systems of federalism for all communities of Canada. It is part of the process of defining ourselves and of developing a national identity for this dynamic young country of ours.
Let us hope and pray that the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future, created by the Prime Minister last week, will be truly successful in its mission to rekindle the vision of a strongly united Canada in the minds of all Canadians as we proceed on our historic constitutional journey in the months that lie ahead.
As others have said, the Fathers of Confederation had to establish the basis for a national identity that would encompass divergent interests and needs. They were successful, but they could only begin the task. It was up to future generations such as ours to continue to build on the past and to shape the nation of their dreams and the nation of our dreams. That process is far from over.

November 6, 1990
Private Members' Business
As we have known in recent years and months, there has been pain and discord, and there remains much healing to do because of the often painful emotions which have been stirred in the heat of debate. Nevertheless, I believe that we will come out of this process much stronger and much more committed in all ways than ever to staying together as a united Canada.
Yes, we Canadians do have our differences from coast to coast, from region to region, from culture to culture, and from language to language. And, yes, we sometimes argue and we debate vigorously about those differences. And, yes, sometimes we find the ties that bind are either too tight or too loose. But the longer we stay together, the more, I believe, we appreciate what we can gain through this great Canadian experiment; this marriage of provinces, territories and regions; and this embracing of two official languages and so many cultures.
The motion before us today to honour the role of Charlottetown in the Canadian nation has great merit. Such recognition is important, not only to Charlottetown, and not just to Prince Edward Island, but to all of Canada. To pass this motion will help us to celebrate the great achievement of nationhood which we enjoy, and it will help to guide us toward a better understanding of our origins.
I agree with my colleagues who have said that we must take care to be correct about the wording. If we were merely to say that Charlottetown is the birthplace of Canada, we would be losing sight of some very important historical facts. The term "Canada" was long in use before 1864 when the the Charlottetown Conference brought colonial representatives together to discuss the idea of a federation of British North America which has become Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in the 16th century the word "Canada" was used as a synonym to describe France's colonies in New France. Explorer Jacques Cartier even referred to the St. Lawrence River as the river of Canada. The first Canada therefore was a French Canada, and the foundations of this nation were laid mostly by French-speaking settlers.

Our Canadian nation actually took root in the soil of Quebec. Later, the Constitutional Act of 1791 created
two political entities bearing the name Canada. These entities, Upper and Lower Canada, were the origins of the modem provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
In 1841, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the two entities were joined for a few decades into one province of Canada. It was a delegation from that province which met with the maritime representatives in Charlottetown in 1864 to propose the idea of a federation. In fact, originally the Charlottetown Conference was only to consider a union between Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, my own home province. The government of the Province of Canada at that time asked permission to send representatives to that meeting. It then put forward its proposal for a larger union.
The practical details of the union were hammered out a month later at a conference in Quebec City. This meeting agreed to 72 resolutions, known as the Quebec Resolutions, which became the basis of the statute that would unite some of the British North American provinces into the confederation called Canada.
The vision presented was of a new nation from sea to sea, one of great national wealth and potential. It would offer both the security of a federal parliamentary system and the autonomy over provincial affairs. It would give the people of Quebec more control over language and education, and would recognize Quebec's separate legal system, the civil code, which remains in practice in that province today.
At the very time that our U.S. neighbours were engaged in a bloody civil war, our founding communities were seeking the peaceful road to union. They were reaching out to one another in a spirit of compromise, generosity and trust. Can we do less today?
Embedded in our first constitutional document was recognition of the distinct nature of Quebec. We continue to respect the original pact with Quebecers in Canada and we seek to strengthen its meaning in today's circumstances.
Being precise about the details of history helps to remind us how much we really are a blend of different cultures and traditions and how much we owe to both the French and the English-speaking elements of our roots.
November 6, 1990

I want to support the amended motion that Charlottetown be designated the birthplace of Confederation. Not only was Charlottetown the host city for the Fathers of Confederation in 1864, but it also contains the original building in which the leaders met. Its restored sector beautifully preserves the atmosphere of those times.
Just last year, Prince Edward Islanders celebrated the 125th anniversary of the 1864 Conference with festivals, exhibitions, and theatre productions. Although that anniversary year is over, it is still important to keep the memory of 1864 alive. We must ensure that Canadians do remember those first crucial steps toward the formation of our country, particularly as we draw closer to 1992 which will be the 125th anniversary of our Confederation. It will certainly be a great occasion for celebration all across Canada.
We have much to celebrate. We have created something great here on this continent. Our different cultures and communities have maintained their distinct identities while enriching one another.

The union of French and English Canada was the basis of the vision of a tolerant, humane, generous, forwardlooking and open Canada. Of course we did not quite achieve all these goals. Indeed we have covered a lot of ground since that first pathetic debate at Charlottetown, but we still have a long way to go.

In closing, it is up to all Canadians to continue the work of reaching out to one another and building a new climate of trust and understanding that can only come from faith and goodwill of every citizen of the country. A nation is based on much more than a constitution. It is based on a sense of community. We, in the House, have a special responsibility. We must all work in our respective constituencies to heal the wounds, to spread the message of hope, to strengthen the trust, and to ensure the future unity of this great country, Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most pleased to stand in the House today and speak to Private Members' Motion No. 498, as put forward by my honourable colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough, and
Private Members' Business
amended by another hon. colleague, the hon. member for Cardigan.
The motion reads, and I quote:
That in the opinion of this House, the city of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island should be designated as the "Birthplace of Canada" to mark the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of the 1864 Charlottetown Conference of the Fathers of Confederation.
One might ask why I, the member of Parliament for Nepean, Ontario would be speaking on this motion today. Prince Edward Island is my birthplace. As a native islander-I was bom in Summerside, Prince Edward Island-as the daughter of a North Bedeque potato farmer, as the descendant of ancestors who arrived on the island in the year 1779, as a former student of Prince of Wales College in Charlottetown, and as an expatriate sister of two brothers and a sister still residing on the island, I feel more than qualified, and especially honoured, to speak to this motion.
P.E.I. is probably one of the most unique provinces of Canada. It has never lost its sense of history. There is tremendous pride in its heritage and its residents have gone to great lengths to preserve this heritage. However, there is one stone that has been left unturned and that is the purpose of the motion before us here this afternoon.
Mr. Speaker, I will make note here that my research material has been taken largely from historical documents written by Reverend Francis W. P. Bolger, PhD., St. Dunstan's University, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
In the Legislative Council Chamber in the Provincial Building in Charlottetown on September 8, 1864, the guest speaker concluded his speech to conference delegates by saying:
I believe, from all that I can learn that the Provinces will, ere long, be one great country or nation, from the Pacific to the Atlantic. Never before was there such an important meeting as this held in the history of British America; and it may yet be said that here, in little Prince Edward Island, was that union formed which has produced one of the greatest nations on the face of God's earth.
Fifty years later, the government of the day erected a bronze tablet in commemoration of Confederation, on which was engraved:
Unity is strength. In the hearts and minds of the delegates who assembled in this room on September 1, 1864, was bom the Dominion of Canada. Providence being their guide, they built better than they knew.

November 6, 1990
Private Members' Business
Listen to the words and think of those words that were used: "Provinces will be one great nation".
This was said way back in those years, Mr. Speaker.
They said: "The Union has produced one of the greatest nations on earth". They also said: "Unity is strength". We need to reflect on those words today.
At a time in our history when some are questioning Canada as a federation, I believe it is time to renew our vows, so to say, as a nation; Motion M-498 will do just that.
In April 1864, the three maritime provinces met with the idea that a union of the three would be beneficial to all.
Interestingly enough it was P.E.I. which opposed such a union as it was feared they might lose their independence.
However, they did take the initiative to explore whether the "Canadian" delegation-and the Canadian delegation was referred to by the member for Fredericton-Upper Canada and Lower Canada, would meet with the maritime premiers to determine if a union of the whole of the British North American provinces was feasible. It was agreed that there would be a meeting and Charlottetown was chosen as the location.
The Charlottetown Conference opened on September 1, 1884. John A. Macdonald made a long speech in favour of the union.
The "Canadians" were indifferent as to whether the maritimes entered individually or as a unit.
The shelving of the maritime union actually happened during the conference and this in turn helped the cause of Confederation.
A very important result of the conference was that it was unanimously agreed that a federal union of all of the British North American provinces would be advantageous if it could be based upon principles that were just and equitable to the several provinces. I think that holds true today, Mr. Speaker.
The delegates went so far as to agree provisionally on certain principles which should be incorporated into the larger plan. On the consummation of the union, all debts would be assumed by the federal government.
It is abundantly clear that the Charlottetown Conference did accomplish a great deal with respect to the
future constitution of Canada. The agreement that a federal union was feasible and the broad outline of a constitution for such a union was indeed a major accomplishment.
The adjustment of the details was destined to be a painful task, but an important step had already been taken.
The most important effect of the conference was that the deliberations at Charlottetown had revealed that there was sufficient agreement on the principle of a federal union to justify the continuance of the discussion in a subsequent formal meeting at Quebec.
The conference provided an opportunity for the leading statesmen of the several provinces to become acquainted with each other and to cement the personal relationships that are intangible necessities in any formal negotiation. Moreover, the broad agreements reached facilitated the completion of a federal scheme at the Quebec Conference. John A. Macdonald, who may be regarded as the architect of the Canadian federal union, made references to the Charlottetown Conference in the Canadian Confederation debates in 1865, which can be regarded as very adequate analyses of the results of the conference.
John A. Macdonald asserted in his first debate on February 6, 1865, that "the broad agreements reached at the Charlottetown conference greatly facilitated the acceptance of the federal union at Quebec".
Later, in the same debate, he claimed that if the Charlottetown Conference had not been held, federal union could well have been delayed for many years. Macdonald's tributes to this conference placed its importance as a prerequisite to federal union beyond question.
From these considerations, I trust that you will agree that the Charlottetown Conference was a very important step in the formation of our Canadian nation.
I regret, however, that few accounts of Canadian history recognize its importance. Too often references to the Charlottetown conference limit their focus to the following type of remarks: "The Fathers of Confederation met in Charlottetown in September 1864, and there it was decided to have a formal conference in Quebec in October".
November 6, 1990

The author I referred to earlier in my opening comments, Reverend Francis W. R Bolger, believes that such a cursory treatment of the conference leaves a tremendous gap in our knowledge of the story of Confederation.
Although the political baby, "Confederation", was not born at the Charlottetown Conference, Dr. Bolger felt that the provision of the "cradle" was of great significance and should be recognized as such in Canadian history.
I have related the historical events surrounding the conference as related by Reverend Dr. Bolger and I am most grateful for his writings. He has been widely recognized as the pre-eminent scholar for the island's history. It is only right that his writings be used by myself and written into the House of Commons Hansard in perpetuity for all to see.
The 125th anniversary of Confederation will be celebrated in 1992 and it is hoped that this narrative will help Canadians better understand and be more aware of their history.
Today we see a fractured Canada. We see tensions between provinces. We hear of provinces talking of their independence and separating from the federal union. We need to find unifying symbols that will again continue to tie us together.
The recognition of Charlottetown as the birthplace of Confederation will have a profound economic benefit to the island, but it will also reaffirm Prince Edward Island's commitment to Canada and Canada's commitment to the island and its capital, Charlottetown.
It has been a real privilege for me to speak here today in the House on this motion. As referred to by the member for Fredericton, I think that this is one of the glues that can help tie this nation together. I think we should reflect very seriously on the intent of the motion and what it is intended to do.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a brief word in support of the motion which is before the House. Other hon. members have done a good job of recounting the history of pre-Confederation, Confederation itself and post-Confederation. They have given us a lot of welcome advice on the things we ought to keep in mind at this particular juncture in Canadian history.
Private Members' Business
I might say that at least in my history lessons that I received at school, Charlottetown did receive full credit. I had not heard about the subsequent conference in Quebec. I think that Charlottetown certainly has received a good deal of the credit for being the birthplace of Confederation.
I think it is a time for us to remember that what Sir John A. Macdonald called the happy opportunity of founding a great nation still is an opportunity, an opportunity that always has to be worked on, that is a continuing opportunity that no country, no nation can take for granted. I think there is an element in the Canadian consciousness whereby we assume that our country is different from other countries, that it is not exposed to all the tensions and travail of human history. I think we found out, I hope early enough, that we are not and that it takes a lot of work to keep the country together, particularly one as large and as diverse as Canada.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to bring to the attention of the House the remarks made by the now retired Secretary General of the Commonwealth, Sonny Ramphal. He appeared before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade in what was sort of a parting testimony, if you like, at the time when we did not yet know the fate of the Meech Lake Accord.
Whatever our individual or our collective opinion might be about the Meech Lake Accord, I think that what he had to say to the committee at that time is still instructive, even in the post-Meech Lake failure period. What he said was this, and it was very much like something I had to say in earlier debates on the Constitution in the early 1980s: if Canada, a country with so much going for it, with a strong democratic tradition, with a history of solving problems co-operatively and peacefully, cannot reconcile within ourselves the problems that come from having a country with more than one linguistic community and a variety of peoples from all around the world, if we who, if you like, are the prototype of the world, if we, with everything going for us, cannot determine how to live together and somehow fragment and break apart, then this will be a terrible signal indeed for the rest of the world.

Adjournment Debate
I think it is something that we do not keep in mind often enough, and that is that a lot rides in terms of moral and political example on how Canadians deal with each other. For a long time, the nations of the world have looked to Canada and its experience as an example of where people of different cultures, different languages and different traditions, have been able to come together and form one country.
If we now, at a time when the world more than ever needs to learn that lesson, unlearn ours, then we will not only be doing a disservice to ourselves, to the heritage which so many people have pointed out this afternoon and to the future, as it pertains to our own children and grandchildren, but we will be doing a disservice to the world because we will be saying: "Even here in Canada with everything going for us, we were not able to manage it; you guys should forget it". I think that is a terrible message to send out to the rest of the planet.
