Last May, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship to explain to us why he was unable to hire representatives of visible minorities, particularly women. I also asked him to tell us when he thought he would remedy such a deplorable situation.
The minister being absent, the Acting Prime Minister answered that objectives for 1991 would indicate an increase of 3.8 per cent in the number of visible minority representatives in the public service.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that this reply does not really provide us with any guarantee as to the number of women from visible minorities who will have jobs in the Public Service.

I would like to quote an answer that the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship gave during a talk show on multicultural policy in Alberta on May 14 of this year.
November 6, 1990

To the question "You're trying to create equal opportunity, aren't you", the minister responded:
Equal opportunity. Equal access. You have to have the ability, of course. When I look around, and when we see there is absolutely no opportunity and no (way) for any of the visible minorities to be included, of course we have difficult police-racial-minority relations.
We ask that (an) institution examine not only its own program of cross-cultural understanding but find a way to include some of them within (for example) the police department, so that there will be a better relationship and there will be an ability of the police and collegiality to understand how minority and community cultures think.
Let me turn it around. You've got a visible minority population in Toronto of 20 per cent. Go to any institution. Do you find them in relative numbers? Not at all -So we need a little catching up to do."
I would like to know how the minister hopes to have a better participation from the institutions in the integration of visible minorities, and women in particular, when his own department does not lead the way.

Mr. Speaker, if there is a Department which should have a large proportion of visible minority people, it is that of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. If this agency wants to get results, it should set an example.
How could it ask institutions to hire at least the minimal percentage required by the government when this very government does not meet its own standards?
If it is important for this agency to show leadership with regard to visible minorities, Mr. Speaker, it is also vital that it should open the way for women. This does not mean doubling the clerical staff establishment. It is important for women to assume more and more decision-making positions. There are many competent women. The government should have the political will to seek them out, accept to pay the price and stop being afraid of them. If the minister is really sincere, he will find the way to hire in his own department women from visible minorities in executive positions. Only then will he be in a position to require others to meet the standards.

If multiculturalism is the reality of this nation, as the minister said, how does he intend to reflect this reality in his own department?
Adjournment Debate The minister affirmed the following:
I guess my obligation is, in addition to helping people in their awareness-to reach out and seek the partnerships; it is to challenge every institution of the community so that it examines itself and makes sure that it provides opportunity for the full Canadian diversity to participate.
Is he asking others to do what he is incapable of doing? [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I realize that departmental staff cannot be changed overnight, but the Minister was given responsibility for Multiculturalism and Citizenship some time ago. How much longer do we have to wait to see visible minorities and women in senior management?
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if we want things to happen, we must clearly identify what objectives should be reached and when. It is too easy to say that things have improved and that we are making headway. Going along at a snail's pace is not exactly what I would call progress, but perhaps that is why this issue is still on the agenda.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Minister responsible for Multiculturalism and Citizenship will soon be able to tell us that a number of management positions, in his own department, for instance, are held by representatives of visible minorities. Meanwhile, we in the Liberal Party will continue to put pressure on the government to achieve balanced representation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of TVansport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to address the question put by the hon. member opposite on May 14 regarding the employment opportunities for visible minorities within the public sector.
The federal government is strongly committed to the principle of equality in the work place and to fair employment practices over all. Awareness, dedication and a solid, concrete plan of action have been the essence of the government's approach. We have sought to ensure that all employees are free from discriminatory attitudes that stifle individual productivity and limit personal growth.
There has been a comprehensive program of employment equity in place since 1983. It clearly requires that all government departments and agencies develop action

15236	COMMONS DEBATES	November 6, 1990
Adjournment Debate
plans, including specific numerical targets for improving the representation of designated groups.
Over the years, significant progress has been made in promoting the employment of members of visible minority groups in the Public Service. As of 1989 the number of visible minorities within the Public Service had risen to 6,829, compared to 4,159 in 1985. Over the four-year period the percentage rate has nearly doubled from 1.7 per cent to 3 per cent of the total work force.
Treasury Board has also established the Visible Minority Employment Program to recruit members of visible minorities actively. It has allocated more than $15 million and 400 person-years for the period 1988 through 1993. In addition, an advisory committee on the employment of visible minorities is in place to address issues of concern to visible minorities.
The present government clearly recognizes the unfortunate reality that certain segments of Canada's population are still confronted with serious disadvantages in the job market. That is why the government has determined to take a pro-active role by seeking to create a workforce in the Public Service inclusive of aboriginal peoples, members of visible minority groups, persons with disabilities, and women. They are a part of this nation's work force and deserve to be optimistic about their future.
The President of the Treasury Board indicated that considerable progress has been made in recent years on this front. At present, an increase of 3.8 per cent in minority representation within the Public Service is being projected for 1991.
With respect to the representation of women in the Public Service, we have redoubled our efforts. All major categories within the Public Service have experienced steady increases in the number of women participating since 1984 when the government was first elected. In keeping with this, it is equally vital that women be represented in the upper levels of the Public Service and in positions of authority. The representation of women in the management category has increased from 7 per cent in 1984 to 14.1 per cent in 1989.
The government stands firmly by its commitment to promote the increased representation of visible minorities and women within the Public Service. More than
ever it is determined to ensure that the equality of opportunity and access guaranteed by our Employment Equity Act, our Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and our Canadian Multiculturalism Act is reflected within the Public Service.
Yes, there is still room for improvement, and we in the government are the first ones to admit it. We are determined to spare no effort in ensuring that the Public Service of the 1990s and beyond reflect the rich diversity and broad experience of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, when I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration last week if she would consider granting retroactive parental benefits to January, 1990, she gave me a very curt and blunt answer. She simply said "no".
Since then we have seen in the press many articles referring to the current confusion with regard to which new parents may qualify or not for these benefits. I understand the problems involved in putting together a new program, but I must again point out to the minister something she might have forgotten; pregnant women

cannot put off giving birth until everyone has been properly briefed on the issue.
Not only is the minister creating tension at what should be a joyous occasion, but she is also hiding behind overworked government employees to avoid doing something.
In committee on October 25, the Deputy Minister and Chairman of the Department of Employment and Immigration said there would be newspaper ads on November 12 and brochures mailed to people currently on claim to inform them.
Meanwhile, it appears that employees of Employment Centres in Canada are being kept in the dark, as well as the Canadian public. The minister's office is saying on the one hand that in some cases parents of babies bom before November 18 could still receive the parental benefits, providing they do not start a claim before the implementation date or even in some cases, if there had been a claim but the woman had gone back to work for 20 weeks, she could then apply for the benefits.
Other scenarios have also been outlined by the minister's office, but it seems that her office has not been able to make their wishes known across the country.
One must wonder, Mr. Speaker, what it will take for those in the front line, when you consider the massive lay-offs due to the recession. Clearly under the present conditions, there will be longer delays for people before they can receive payment.
When this is added to a complex, and I want to point out, mostly unfair reform of the unemployment insurance system, things can only get worse. Given the fact that the minister has not specified what could happen to people who are not fully informed prior to the implementation of these benefits, she is preparing another bureaucratic nightmare.
She should reconsider her previous decision and make parental benefits retroactive, if not all the way back to January 1, at least to when Royal Assent was given, to allow more people to qualify and also to simplify the process.
Given the current situation, she should also consider hiring more staff to expedite the process. The union representing employees at the Employment Centre, PSAC, has asked for an increase in staff for the past two
Adjournment Debate
years. What kind of a nightmare are these employees, who now have shortfalls, going to be facing with even more problems with these new applicants?
To make matters more difficult, she added some small benefits such as the parental benefit. I want to add that no one can argue that granting parental benefits is a bad thing, but in introducing this it should not be done on the backs and at the expense of other unemployed workers.

Last week, the National Anti-Poverty Organization, the Mouvement action-chomage de Montreal and the Ontario Coalition Against Poverty denounced the changes to the Unemployment Insurance scheme as one of the worst attacks against wage-earners.
We may well wonder if the figures quoted by Deputy Minister Kroeger in committee were a figment of his imagination.
The Deputy Minister claimed that, according to some studies, only 30,000 people would be affected by the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Yet, according to the figures provided by the Quebec Department of Employment, nearly 60,000 people will be affected by this reform.

Welfare cases in metro Toronto are expected to almost double from last year. The tightening of federal unemployment insurance rules is being labelled as one of the causes.
We also read in the minutes of the committee that the training aspect of the bill will not be in effect until January 1, 1991. The government has been collecting higher premiums since January of 1990, yet the programs are not in place. The government is making money on the backs of those who can least afford it. The government had an alternative but they clearly refused to look at one; the same way they refused to look at all other alternatives to the GST.
In Australia the government has decided to legislate a national training tax system, known as the training guarantee. This scheme will ensure that all Australian firms with an annual payroll of over $200,000 will spend a minimum of 1 per cent of payroll on approved training in 1990-91 and then the minimum will rise to 1.5 per cent of payroll after two years. There is an alternative that

Adjournment Debate
would have achieved the goal of maintaining and upgrading a highly skilled labour force.
The minister thought she would be better off with the easy way out, by taking away funding from a much needed program, particularly in these difficult times. She took the easy way out and working families must deal with the consequences.
We are looking for a favourable solution to this problem and I hope that the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration will rise and offer us a solution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address some of the points made by the hon. member opposite. The government, and I am sure, most Canadians are happy that the Senate has finally seen fit to pass Bill C-21. Indeed, some of the comments that the hon. member makes today are directly related to the measures in that bill that are seen as improvements by many people in this country.
In respect of the member's comment that they implementation of Bill C-21 is a nightmare in some cases, I would appreciate some details rather than general allegations. My information is that the implementation of the bill is proceeding on schedule and that the local offices are well able to cope with the problems they face.
In so far as the provision of parental benefits is concerned, I would be remiss if I did not point out, for information purposes at least, that it is this government that saw fit to introduce them. We do not need any lessons from the opposition as to their appropriateness. The parental provisions of Bill C-21 represent a significant advance over the existing legislation, and have been introduced to recognize the legitimate concerns of Canadians who find themselves in the position of starting families and wishing to maintain an active attachment to the labour force at the same time.
The hon. member seems to think that Canadian families have paid for parental benefits since January, 1990. Nothing could be further from the truth. He did not correctly understand the minister's first press conference on Bill C-21 in April, 1989 and subsequent explanations on many occasions.
She has explained clearly and repeatedly that the economies realized from the new provisions respecting entrance, duration, and voluntary leaving employment without just cause would be poured back into the program in order to finance the significant improvements being made in the areas of training, parental benefits, benefits to persons over the age of 65, and so on. The increased premiums are not paying for the program enrichment.
The setting of the premium rate was announced by the Minister of Finance in his budget of April, 1989. It is in no way tied to the more generous benefits contained in Bill C-21. In fact, as the minister and her officials testified before the committees in the House of Commons and in the Senate, the freezing of the premium rates for 1990, 1991, and 1992 is designed to soften the impact on a yearly basis of the introduction of the Labour Force Development Strategy as a whole.
We also clearly said that if there were any deficits in the UI account were to accrue, the Government of Canada would-as it has done in the past-advance the necessary funds to ensure that the account is able to continue to pay the UI benefits that Canadians need.
I would also like to comment on the issue of retroactivity. The hon. member wants to know why the parental benefits are not made retroactive to January, 1990. No one would be happier than this government if this could have been the case. Indeed, the Labour Force Development Strategy was developed so that the parental benefits would come into effect on January 1, 1990.
However, the Senate of Canada, for reasons still best known to itself, chose to delay the legislation for almost a year. Thus, instead of coming into force on January 1, 1990 as we had planned, the parental benefits provisions will only have effect as of November 18, 1990.
People such as the hon. member who want to know why this took so long are best advised to pose their question elsewhere as the intent of the government in this respect has been clear and consistent. I regret that the passage of the bill was delayed so long and I believe that the hon. member will, upon reflection, feel the same way.
November 6, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to you for this opportunity to take part in this debate on the adjournment motion about the issue which I raised with the Minister of Finance on October 11, as reported on page 141 of Hansard. My question had to do with the great many jobs being lost every day, including 3,000 at Air Canada, 1,500 at CN and 3,000 at Esso. To date, I should like to add the 700 lost at Marine Industries and approximately 1,000 at Kratt & Whitney in Longueuil. Also, the number of banruptcies is on the rise. A short while ago, as a result of several questions from the opposition, the Minister of Finance finally recognized that we are now in a recession.
What I found astonishing, Mr. Speaker, in the Minister's response to my question was this, and I quote:
[ -] Surely he acknowledges that the biggest problem that Air Canada has today is the increase in oil prices, which in turn has been caused by the international problem in the Middle East right now.
There is indeed a crisis in the Persian Gulf, Mr. Speaker, but that is not why Air Canada laid-off 3,000 people. I think the lay-offs are due to a much deeper crisis. It has to do, first of all, with the Minister of Finance's high dollar monetary policy. Tourism, for example, had a disastrous season. Suffice it to quote Claude Picher who was saying the following, just a few days ago, in an article published in La Presse on October 23. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read part of that interesting article:
Tburistic nightmare
A harsh and inescapable reality is emerging from behind the official optimism of the travel promotion industry: Canada is headed for its worst deficit ever, and by far in The Tburism industry! The most recent statistics indicate that the peak season-July and August-is a disaster. If past trends are any indication we can already forecast that Canada's 1990 tourism deficit will be around $4.4 billion-an increase of 26 per cent over 1989 and 62 per cent over 1988. Even accounting for inflation the deterioration is spectacular. You will have a good idea of the damage if I point out that, at the time, 1988 had been labelled a disaster year!
Of course, you can always say that Canada is used to that. Year in and year out our tourism deficit is rather significant. Particularly troubling this year-never mind the huge deficit-are the summer figures.
Adjournment Debate
And there is more in the same article, Mr. Speaker. Here are specific figures:
In July, foreign visitors-Americans mostly-made 5.6 million
trips to Canada. This may look good, but it indicates a decline of 4.7
per cent over the same month last year.
So, Mr. Speaker, clearly Air Canada's problems have nothing to do with the oil crisis, but they can indeed be traced right back to the economic crisis created by the Minister of Finance, a made-in-Canada crisis. Should he stubbornly maintain his high-dollar monetary policy you can be sure that tourist-particularly Americans who usually come up to Canada in droves-will find our costs prohibitive and travel elsewhere. We are already beginning to see the economic impact on that industry.
Mr. Speaker, to prove that these economic policies are a disaster for Canada, we had the same day-I don't know whether it was a day for bad news-the 23rd of October, another article in the same La Presse, intitled "Competitivity decreasing in Canada". In the 1980s, Mr. Speaker, we were ranked second, but we are now sixth.
This is unacceptable! How can we stay competitive, now that we are in the 1990s and that the 21st century is fast approaching? If the minister sticks to its policies, we are sure to have a "made in Canada" economic disaster. He often refers back to the years 1981-82, but we were going through an international crisis then. What we are facing now is a made in Canada crisis resulting from the monetary policy of the Minister of Finance, the high Canadian dollar policy which is hurting the tourism industry terribly as we have said earlier. The high interest rates policy, which results in a much stronger Canadian dollar, is most harmful to Canadian manufacturers who are unable to keep up with the competition because of high financing costs. They must incorporate those additionnal costs into their operations and that is why prices are increasing.
That is all there is to it, Mr. Speaker! And when the Minister asked me if I had any suggestions, I said to him that he should first lower the interest rates. He should do it as soon as possible so as to restore confidence within the industry, create employment and have people working again. This would in turn bring about a viable economy and we could consider the future with some hope.

November 6, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time is up now. I hope that the Parliamantaiy Secretary, who will be answering on behalf of the Finance Minister, will give us some indication that a considerable reduction is to be anticipated when the Bank of Canada announces the prime rate this week, as it does every Thursday, so that Canadians can continue hoping for a better future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government recognizes that the Canadian economy is now going through an adjustment period that is a source of difficulties for many Canadians.
However, given the excessively rapid growth of these last years, the present economic slowdown should surprise nobody nor create a feeling of crisis.
This is normal in a period of strong growth when the demand for goods and services outpaces the productive capacity of the economy.
The vigorous expansion of our economy during the last seven years made for a tight supply on the labour and goods markets, resulting in destructive inflationary pressures. Had we not reacted immediately to dampen inflation, pressures could have built up in our economy and it would have been much more difficult and costly to eliminate them later on.
That is why this government developed and implemented wise fiscal and economic policies in order to better balance demand and supply while alleviating inflationary pressures. This will lead to a drop in interest rates and a return to a balanced and sustained growth.
We are in the middle of the adjustment period. We are aware that these adjustment periods always bring some real difficulties. However, it is important that Canadians recognize that these changing economic conditions ease the inflationary pressures that push up prices and business costs, erode competitiveness and jeopardize the jobs of Canadian workers.

I want to assure the hon. member that we are fully sensitive to how important the course of monetary conditions will be for the operations of business and our economy as a whole. Many voices have called on the government to lower interest rates in order to revive economic activity and avoid further job losses. However, attempts to create employment through an inflationary monetary policy would be self-defeating. It is critical that all participants in our economy recognize that the government's scope to alter monetary conditions depends directly on the continued reduction of inflationary pressures.
I wish to assure the hon. member that the government remains committed to the economic agenda followed since 1984. It is also creating the conditions for sustainably lower interest rates and balanced sustained growth.
